- Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially in the first 5–10 days, then gradually converges toward true values — suggesting a lag or delayed response to actual market dynamics.
- After sharp spikes in true values (e.g., 53.86, 53.63), model forecasts overshoot and remain elevated for several days, failing to correct quickly — indicating poor handling of volatility or momentum decay.
- Model exhibits strong mean reversion bias: it tends to forecast values that are too high relative to recent history, especially when true values dip sharply — suggesting it underweights recent downward momentum.
- Forecasts are overly optimistic in the short term (1–3 days) and overly pessimistic in the long term (10+ days) — suggesting a need to adjust for horizon-specific volatility clustering.
- Model fails to capture the “tail” of the distribution — particularly when true values dip below 50, it underestimates the magnitude of the drop, leading to persistent overestimation.
- Model shows a tendency to smooth out volatility — it underreacts to sudden true value changes, especially when true values are below 50, leading to persistent overestimation.
- Model overestimates the “mean” of the distribution — especially when true values are clustered around 47–50, it forecasts higher values, suggesting a need to adjust for baseline drift or seasonality.
- Model underestimates the “tail” of the distribution — particularly when true values are below 45, it fails to recognize the risk of sharp drops, leading to overconfidence in forecasts.
- Model exhibits a “memory” bias — it overweights recent history, especially when true values are below 50, leading to persistent overestimation.
- Model underestimates the “volatility” of the distribution — particularly when true values are clustered around 50–55, it fails to recognize the risk of sharp drops, leading to overconfidence in forecasts.
